title: Pentagon Drops $135B on Subs and Missiles, China Demotes Hypersonics to Smaller Ships, BAE Lands £5.9B Dreadnought Deal
subhead: The Pentagon awarded $135 billion in mega-contracts for submarines and interceptors as CSIS reports US Patriot stockpiles have fallen below 1,000 missiles. China revealed the YJ-20 hypersonic missile launching from a Type 052D destroyer, and BAE Systems secured a £5.9B contract for the UK's next-generation nuclear-armed submarines.

sections.heading: Pentagon Commits $135B in Single Day as Stockpiles Run Dry
sections.body:
The US Defense Department announced two of the largest procurement contracts in American history on July 29, together worth roughly $135 billion. Lockheed Martin received a $59 billion, seven-year deal to triple production of PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptor missiles, raising annual output from roughly 600 to 2,000 by 2030, according to Bloomberg and the Hindu Business Line. The deal extends an April contract with a $53.86 billion modification. Lockheed plans to hire 650 additional workers, building a Patriot workforce of 1,850 at its Camden, Arkansas plant.

Simultaneously, General Dynamics Electric Boat and Huntington Ingalls Industries received submarine construction contracts worth up to $76.6 billion — the largest shipbuilding award in modern American history. This covers nine Block VI Virginia-class attack submarines (equipped with expanded Tomahawk cruise missile capacity) and five Columbia-class ballistic-missile submarines, plus shipyard infrastructure improvements. Rep. Joe Courtney called it the 'biggest shipbuilding award in modern American history,' noting the contracts secure work through the late 2030s and are boosted by the AUKUS agreement for selling Virginia-class subs to Australia.

These awards follow Lockheed's earlier $35 billion THAAD interceptor production contract and the Defense Production Act invocation by Trump last month to remove procurement obstacles. L3Harris Technologies also announced it would accelerate production of solid rocket motors for both PAC-3 MSE and THAAD missiles. According to CSIS, roughly 10,000 new defense and aerospace companies have entered the market in the last two years, with startups attracting $120 billion in 2025 alone.
sections.whyItMatters: The scale of these contracts reflects a permanent shift to wartime industrial posture. The US has used two-thirds of its Patriot interceptors since the Iran war began, and even tripling production to 2,000 per year may not suffice for a prolonged conflict — let alone one against a near-peer. The submarine contracts also lock in AUKUS submarine deliveries to Australia through the 2030s.

sections.heading: CSIS: US Patriot Stockpiles Down to Under 1,000 Missiles
sections.body:
The Center for Strategic and International Studies reported that the US has used up two-thirds of its Patriot interceptor stockpile since the Iran war began. Pre-war inventories stood at over 2,700 Patriot and THAAD missiles combined; as of July 28, available Patriot interceptors had fallen to between 759 and 827, according to CSIS estimates cited by the New York Post. THAAD inventories dropped from 452 pre-war to between 232 and 262 — a 38% decline.

The numbers have continued to deteriorate even during the current pause in US strikes on Iran. During the recent flare-up, Patriot interceptors fell from 1,030 at the start of the ceasefire to the current range, with each PAC-3 MSE costing roughly $3.9 million and taking up to two years to manufacture. CSIS warned there are 'no good alternatives to Patriot and THAAD for ballistic missile defense' and that further stockpile depletion could change how the US responds to attacks on its Middle East bases.

At least three Iranian missiles penetrated US defenses at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan earlier this month, killing three US soldiers — a sign that the interception rate, while nearly perfect in early months, is starting to slip as interceptors thin out.
sections.whyItMatters: The data quantifies what the $59B Patriot contract is trying to fix. Two-thirds depletion in five months raises the question of whether the US could sustain even its current operational tempo, let alone a broader conflict. The two-year manufacturing lead time means replacements won't arrive fast enough to change the trajectory.

sections.heading: China Reveals YJ-20 Hypersonic Launch From Smaller Destroyer
sections.body:
China revealed for the first time the launch of its YJ-20 hypersonic anti-ship ballistic missile from a Type 052D destroyer, according to a state media trailer released July 30 for the PLA documentary 'Zhisheng,' commemorating the 99th anniversary of the army's founding. Bloomberg reports the demonstration signals a significant expansion of the weapon's deployable platform.

The YJ-20 had previously been shown only on the larger Type 055 destroyer, which displaces roughly 12,000 tons. By successfully launching from the smaller 7,500-ton Type 052D — China's most numerous modern destroyer class with over 25 vessels — Beijing is indicating the missile can be fielded across a far larger portion of its fleet. This means more ships in more places can threaten adversary vessels with hypersonic anti-ship weapons.

The YJ-20 is an aeroballistic missile designed to strike ships at hypersonic speeds, making interception extremely difficult with current naval air defense systems. Its wider deployment would complicate US and allied naval planning across the Western Pacific, Indian Ocean, and beyond.
sections.whyItMatters: Hypersonic anti-ship missiles on 25+ destroyers fundamentally changes the threat calculus in the Western Pacific. The Type 052D is China's workhorse destroyer — putting the YJ-20 on it means the weapon is no longer a premium capability reserved for a handful of elite ships. It becomes a distributed, fleet-wide threat.

sections.heading: BAE Systems Wins £5.9B for UK Dreadnought Nuclear Submarines
sections.body:
BAE Systems has been awarded a £5.9 billion ($7.8 billion) contract by the British government to advance work on the country's next generation of nuclear-armed Dreadnought-class submarines, Reuters reported on July 29. The contract funds continued development and construction of the four-boat Dreadnought program, which will replace the current Vanguard class as the UK's continuous at-sea nuclear deterrent.

The Dreadnought program is the UK's largest defense procurement project, with total expected costs exceeding £31 billion for the four submarines. BAE Systems serves as the prime contractor, with work centered at its Barrow-in-Furness shipyard in Cumbria. The first boat is expected to enter service in the early 2030s.

The contract comes as the UK also separately selected Tekever's AR5 drones to replace the troubled Watchkeeper fleet, according to headlines — marking a broader British effort to modernize both its nuclear and conventional capabilities simultaneously.
sections.whyItMatters: The UK is locking in its nuclear deterrent for the next several decades at a time when NATO members are under pressure to increase defense spending. The £5.9B contract ensures the Dreadnought program stays on track, though the total program cost remains one of the UK's biggest long-term fiscal commitments.

sections.heading: SpaceX Lands $1.6B in Space Force Launch Orders as Military Space Demand Surges
sections.body:
SpaceX won $1.6 billion in launch task orders from the US Space Force for 18 Falcon 9 missions through the end of 2027, SpaceNews and Breaking Defense reported. The launches, all from Vandenberg Space Force Base, will deploy satellites for the Space Based Sensing and Targeting (SBST) portfolio — covering missile-warning, communications, and airborne moving target indicator satellites.

The award is the largest publicly disclosed order under the NSSL Phase 3 Lane 1 program, coming just two weeks after the Space Force raised the program's ceiling from $5.6 billion to $17 billion to accommodate a surge in launch demand. SpaceX also holds separate multibillion-dollar contracts for the Space Data Network Backbone ($2.29B) and the Space-Based Airborne Moving Target Indicator program ($4.16B), making it both the launcher and a key satellite supplier.

Separately, the Space Force awarded All Points Logistics a $250 million contract to expand satellite processing capacity at Vandenberg, and Sphinx Defense won a $287 million contract for nuclear satellite communications software. The processing bottleneck at US launch ranges has become a recognized constraint — limited clean rooms and fueling facilities delay missions even when rockets are available.
sections.whyItMatters: The $17B NSSL Phase 3 ceiling — tripled in just one month — shows how fast military space demand is growing. SpaceX is now simultaneously building, launching, and operating key elements of the US military's satellite architecture, concentrating enormous capability in a single commercial contractor.

sections.heading: Russia Floats Out Seventh Yasen-M Submarine as Zircon Reserves Thin
sections.body:
Russia floated out its seventh Yasen-M nuclear attack submarine, the Ulyanovsk, at the Sevmash shipyard on July 28, according to Naval News and other outlets. The Yasen-M class carries Zircon hypersonic cruise missiles, Kalibr land-attack cruise missiles, and Oniks anti-ship missiles, making each boat a multi-role strike platform.

However, the float-out comes amid reports that Russia's Zircon missile reserves are thinning, raising questions about how many of the advanced hypersonic weapons each new submarine will actually carry. Russia has used Zircons sparingly in the Ukraine war, and production of the missile is believed to be constrained by materials shortages and sanctions on key components.

Meanwhile, Russia canceled its annual Navy Day parade in St. Petersburg for the second consecutive year due to Ukrainian drone threats, according to multiple reports. Putin reportedly ordered a probe after the scaled-down celebration — where ships were replaced with a giant banner of a vessel — drew widespread attention to Russia's diminished naval posture.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia is building submarines faster than it can arm them with its most advanced weapons. The Yasen-M hulls are impressive on paper, but without sufficient Zircon missiles, they're multi-role platforms missing their primary capability. The cancelled Navy Day parade is a public admission of vulnerability that undermines the domestic prestige narrative.

sections.heading: Senate Advances Russia-Iran Sanctions Bill as Trump Demands Changes
sections.body:
The US Senate passed a second procedural vote on a sweeping Russia and Iran sanctions bill, with 84 senators voting to advance debate on July 29, according to C-SPAN. The legislation, named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, would tighten economic sanctions on both countries.

However, President Trump demanded changes to the bill on July 29, specifically seeking authority to add Iran tariff provisions, according to multiple outlets. The demand could delay the legislation's passage and reflects ongoing tensions between the White House and Congress over sanctions strategy. Trump's push for tariff authority over Iran comes as the US-Iran conflict enters a pause phase, with the US holding off on airstrikes for a third consecutive night while regional mediators report progress on diplomatic de-escalation.

The bill's momentum reflects broad bipartisan concern about both Russian war sustenance and Iranian proxy networks, but the White House intervention shows the executive branch wants to maintain flexibility over economic pressure tools.
sections.whyItMatters: The sanctions bill has supermajority support, but Trump's last-minute demands could slow it down. The real impact for defense industry is indirect: tighter sanctions on Russia and Iran would further restrict their access to dual-use technology and components, squeezing their ability to produce advanced weapons like the Zircon missile.

bottomLine: The Pentagon just committed $135 billion in a single day to replenish weapons stockpiles and build submarines — the clearest financial signal yet that the US is shifting to a permanent wartime industrial footing. CSIS data shows why: Patriot interceptor inventories have fallen below 1,000, a two-thirds depletion since the Iran war began. Meanwhile, China demonstrated that its most advanced hypersonic anti-ship missile now works on its workhorse destroyer class, not just its premium ships — a fleet-wide threat multiplier. The UK locked in its nuclear deterrent future with a £5.9B Dreadnought contract, SpaceX became the Pentagon's dominant space partner with $1.6B in new launch orders, and Russia floated a submarine it may not be able to fully arm. The global defense industrial base is being reshaped in real time by the demands of active conflicts.
sources: Bloomberg, Reuters, Hindu Business Line, Business Times Singapore, SpaceNews, Breaking Defense, CSIS, New York Post, Stamford Advocate, Naval News, TASS, C-SPAN, Moneycontrol, BISnow, Firstpost
